rationale: Root-caused against a copy of the real failing database (ac2-run2/db/mmetl.db, listing m73020392557): the listing's row and ListingStatusChanges row showed a normal already-sold-from-search listing (IsSold=1, ItemStatus=Sold, one InitialScrape Sold history row) with DetailFetchAttempts=1 and DetailFetchedUtc still null after the failure. Replaying the real captured item page (scratchpad/monthruns/ps5-controller/cache/93EC1A31CBC897FD.html, matched by grepping for m73020392557) through MercariItemPageParser and ItemDetailStore.ApplyItemDetail against a fresh SQLite database with the exact seeded row did NOT reproduce a failure, ruling out a constraint violation or bad data as the cause. Forcing genuine SQLite write-lock contention did reproduce it exactly: holding a manual 'BEGIN IMMEDIATE' transaction on a second raw connection to the same file while ItemDetailStore.ApplyItemDetail's SaveChangesAsync ran on a DbContext from the same IDbContextFactory produced 'Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.DbUpdateException: An error occurred while saving the entity changes. See the inner exception for details.' wrapping 'Microsoft.Data.Sqlite.SqliteException: SQLite Error 5: 'database is locked'.' -- byte-for-byte the same outer message recorded in ScrapeRunIssues for m73020392557. Root cause: ItemDetailStore's IDbContextFactory<EtlDbContext> opens a fresh SQLite connection per operation with no shared cache and no busy-timeout/retry handling, so when a detail-save's write transaction collides with another connection's write transaction (four detail fetches run concurrently, each on its own DbContext/connection against the same file), a transient SQLITE_BUSY/SQLITE_LOCKED is possible and previously surfaced as an unretried DbUpdateException, with only the generic outer EF message recorded (the real SQLite cause was discarded). Two independent fixes were verified: (1) ExceptionIssueMessageFormatter.Describe walks to the innermost exception and appends '(root cause: {Type}: {Message})' to the outer message, applied at both places that record exception-based run issues (ItemDetailFetchService.FetchDetail's catch block and ScrapeRunService.Run's catch block that calls FailRun) so the real SQLite message is never lost again; (2) SqliteBusyRetry.ExecuteAsync wraps ItemDetailStore's two SaveChangesAsync call sites (ApplyItemDetail, MarkDetailFetchFailed) and retries up to 5 times with a short backoff specifically when the innermost exception is a SqliteException with error code 5 (SQLITE_BUSY) or 6 (SQLITE_LOCKED), so a transient lock collision between concurrent detail fetches resolves itself instead of failing the listing. Both are proven red-before-green: with the formatter reverted to plain ex.Message, ItemDetailFetchServiceTests.Should_record_the_innermost_exception_message_and_type_when_the_save_fails and ScrapeRunServiceTests.Should_fail_the_run_with_the_innermost_exception_message_when_the_wrapper_hides_the_cause both fail (asserting the outer generic message contains the inner SqliteException's message/type, which it does not); with SqliteBusyRetry removed from ApplyItemDetail, ItemDetailStoreTests.Should_succeed_when_a_transient_sqlite_lock_blocks_the_save fails with exactly the production DbUpdateException/SqliteException pair (manually confirmed by temporarily reverting each fix and re-running). At base (before implementation) the command fails: ExceptionIssueMessageFormatter, SqliteBusyRetry do not exist, ItemDetailFetchService/ScrapeRunService still record ex.Message directly, and ItemDetailStoreTests has no lock-contention fixture. No test reads git or working-tree state; the real production database copy and captured HTML fixture were used only for interactive root-causing (see criterion-checklist evidence), not as part of the automated suite.
